findings.claim: Verification block asserts the presence of 'update' in the rule-type set but does not assert that update_allows_fetch_and_merge is absent or false. A drift to true weakens the protection while passing all six current assertions.
findings.evidence: script line 133: rule_types=$(jq -r '[.rules[].type] | sort | join(",")') asserts only type names, not rule-specific parameters. The GitHub Rulesets API documents an 'update' rule parameter object with key update_allows_fetch_and_merge (boolean, default false). When set to true, the rule permits fetch-and-merge operations, partially bypassing the update block. No assertion in the script reads .rules[] | select(.type=="update") | .parameters.update_allows_fetch_and_merge. The deletion and non_fast_forward rule types carry no parameters in the current API spec; update is the only rule in the applied set that has a safety-relevant parameter.
findings.impact: A careless operator editing the ruleset via the GitHub UI, or an API-level mutation by an attacker with repo admin access, could set update_allows_fetch_and_merge=true on the scp-tag-protection-renovate-v ruleset. Re-running the configure script would then log 'tag-protection ruleset verified ✓' without detecting the weakening, giving false assurance. The TOCTOU between verification-passes and next re-run is unbounded.
findings.mitigation: Extend the verification block with: update_param=$(printf '%s' "$detail" | jq -r '.rules[] | select(.type=="update") | .parameters.update_allows_fetch_and_merge // false'); if [ "$update_param" != "false" ]; then echo "verification failed: update rule has update_allows_fetch_and_merge=${update_param} (expected false)" >&2; exit 1; fi. This closes the parameter-drift surface without altering the script's idempotency contract.

findings.claim: The existing-ruleset lookup (line 56-57) retains head -1 from the original implementation. R3 fixed head -1 on the POST path (NEW-R3-SAFE-003) but left it unchanged on the listing path. GitHub's Rulesets API does not enforce name uniqueness by contract; two rulesets can share the same name. A malicious duplicate could grant bypass access while the script verifies only the first-in-response-order ruleset.
findings.evidence: script lines 56-57: existing_id=$(printf '%s' "$rulesets" | jq -r --arg name "$RULESET_NAME" '.[] | select(.name == $name) | .id' | head -1). The head -1 silently discards any duplicate entries. FIX-ROUND-3.md §fix-round-3 explicitly acknowledges the listing path retains head -1 ('Existing-ruleset path still uses listing (correct: looking up id of existing ruleset by name)') without adding a duplicate-count guard. A second ruleset named scp-tag-protection-renovate-v with enforcement=active and bypass_actors=[{actor_id: <attacker_team_id>}] would appear in the listing; head -1 would select the correctly-configured one; verification passes; the malicious ruleset remains active and grants bypass to the attacker's actor.
findings.impact: An admin-level actor (or a compromised admin token) can introduce a parallel scp-tag-protection-renovate-v ruleset carrying bypass grants. Re-running the configure script produces a false-positive 'verified ✓' because it inspects only the first-in-listing ruleset. The protection operator believes the system is clean; the bypass remains active indefinitely. Severity is MIN rather than MAJ because exploitation requires pre-existing admin access — the same actor could simply delete the original ruleset — but the false-positive verification output is the distinguishing harm: it actively misleads the operator.
findings.mitigation: Replace the head -1 pipe with an explicit count guard: all_ids=$(printf '%s' "$rulesets" | jq -r --arg name "$RULESET_NAME" '[.[] | select(.name == $name) | .id] | @tsv'); count=$(printf '%s' "$all_ids" | wc -w | tr -d ' '); if [ "$count" -gt 1 ]; then echo "safety abort: $count rulesets named $RULESET_NAME detected; resolve duplicates before proceeding" >&2; exit 1; fi; existing_id=$(printf '%s' "$all_ids" | awk '{print $1}'). This converts the silent head -1 discard into a loud multi-ruleset abort, eliminating the false-positive verification surface.

probes_resolved.rationale: Truncated-JSON scenario: jq parse failure exits non-zero; with set -euo pipefail the assignment at line 97 propagates the non-zero code and the script aborts loudly. Valid-JSON-missing-id scenario: jq -r '.id' outputs literal 'null'; the [ -z "$final_id" ] || [ "$final_id" = "null" ] guard at line 98 catches it and exits 1 with a diagnostic message. No silent acceptance path exists.

Running git rev-parse --show-toplevel outside a git checkout exits non-zero with 'fatal: not a git repository'; cd "" then fails with a shell error. Both errors are loud. In an interactive shell context neither aborts subsequent independent commands automatically, but the subsequent ./scripts/... invocation would fail with 'No such file or directory' — the chain does not silently succeed. The DISPATCH-NOTE.md prerequisites block (lines 70-75) states the requirement explicitly. No new bypass surface.

DISPATCH-NOTE.md lines 70-75 contain the explicit **Prerequisites:** block verbatim as claimed by FIX-ROUND-3.md. The prerequisites note is in the primary runbook document, not only in the fix-round record. NEW-R3-SAFE-005 is genuinely closed.

target_val=$(jq -r '.target // "unknown"') at line 119 maps a missing .target to 'unknown'; the subsequent [ "$target_val" != "tag" ] check then exits 1. Any unusual API response that omits the target field therefore produces a loud abort rather than a silent pass. This is strictly safer than the alternative (.target // "tag") which would silently accept missing-target responses.

structured_review.summary: R3 closures all confirmed. Two new MIN findings surface from round-4 probe work: (1) the update rule's update_allows_fetch_and_merge parameter is not asserted, leaving a drift-weakening surface invisible to the verification block; (2) the existing-ruleset lookup still uses head -1 on the listing path (R3 fixed only the POST path), creating a false-positive verification scenario when a malicious duplicate-name ruleset is present. No CRIT or MAJ findings. Verdict: LGTM_WITH_CONDITIONS. Fixpoint is one small fix round away — both findings are single-assertion additions to the verification block or the listing lookup.
